transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Marcus Hale (Redwood SecEng), Dr. Maya Cortez (CISO, Vespertine), Ethan Park (Head of MLOps), Leah Brooks (Legal), Samir Gupta (Data Privacy)

Summary: quick security & privacy deep-dive focused on data residency, KMS/encryption, audit logging, and explicit confirmation around training on customer data. Vespertine asked for written guarantees, architecture diagrams, and an on-prem pilot to validate no-train behavior and key custody.

Topics: SOC 2 / ISO, RBAC & SSO, audit logs retention and format, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS customer-managed keys, prompt retention and no-train/no-use-for-training commitments, PII/PHI handling, data residency (EU).

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, account lead for Redwood. Uh, big thanks for carving out the time. Priya, Marcus from our side are on to cover the technical and security details. Maya, Ethan, Leah, Samir — over to you for any particular items you'd like us to start with?

[00:18] Dr. Maya Cortez: Hi Jordan. Yeah, thanks. We have a list but top line — we need to confirm that Redwood will not use our prompts or outputs to train models, that any PII/PHI is handled under the DPA, and that we can manage keys (KMS) for at-rest encryption. Also we need audit logs that show request-level metadata for compliance.

[00:38] Jordan Lee: Totally. We'll go through each. Priya, maybe you run the KMS/no-train slide first?

[00:43] Priya Singh: Sure. Um, so first on no-train: Redwood's hosted offering does not train on customer data by default. For enterprise customers we have a contractual no-training clause — basically we do not incorporate customer prompts or outputs into model training pipelines. There are internal notes, uh, exceptions for aggregated telemetry which is anonymized, but, ah, we can commit to a no-training pledge in the contract.

[01:10] Leah Brooks: When you say "aggregated telemetry," can you clarify what is in scope? Particularly anything that could be PII-ish, like user-agent strings tied to IDs?

[01:19] Priya Singh: Good question. Aggregated telemetry is usage-level metrics — token counts, latency histograms, error rates. We strip identifiable fields. We do not include prompt text in that telemetry. If there's anything that looks like PII in a telemetry field it gets redacted before being used for product analytics.

[01:36] Marcus Hale: To add, we can also offer an opt-out flag at the tenant level so telemetry collection is minimized; and for Dedicated/Private deployments telemetry can be turned off entirely.

[01:47] Ethan Park: For the KMS, are we talking about customer-managed keys in cloud KMS, or do you support HSM-backed keys on-prem? Our security team will insist on customer key control if possible.

[01:58] Priya Singh: We support both. Hosted customers can bring their own KMS keys (BYOK) — we integrate with customer KMS through envelope encryption. For Private deployments there's an option to use an HSM or your on-prem KMS. I'll drop a diagram.

[02:13] Dr. Maya Cortez: Can you explain the envelope flow end-to-end? We want to know which components ever see plaintext.

[02:20] Priya Singh: Yeah. High level: client request encrypted to our ingress via TLS; then payload is encrypted with a data key provided by the customer's KMS (envelope key) — Redwood never stores the plaintext data key unencrypted. The runtime decrypts the data key in-memory on GPU host just long enough to run inference, and that key is zeroed from memory after. Only the ephemeral host process touches plaintext. We can provide memory-safety artifacts and a sequence diagram.

[02:46] Samir Gupta: How about logs and cache? Is the KV cache persisted? Could sensitive tokens be left in a cache file?

[02:55] Marcus Hale: Cache behaviour depends on deployment. In Hosted we use a memory-backed KV cache with TTL; nothing is written to disk in the default profile. For Dedicated you can opt into persistent cache for performance, but that is configurable and can be disabled. For Private, you manage persistence. We also salt and encrypt any on-disk artifacts with customer keys when enabled.

[03:15] [interruption] Dr. Maya Cortez: Sorry — what's the retention for request logs? We need logs for 12 months for audits.

[03:22] Jordan Lee: We have configurable retention. Default is 90 days, but enterprise plans support custom retention windows including 12 months. Logs can be exported to your SIEM (Splunk, Sumo, Azure Log Analytics) or we can write to an S3 bucket in your account.

[03:36] Leah Brooks: If logs are exported to S3 in our account, who controls lifecycle and access? We want to ensure Redwood doesn't retain copies.

[03:44] Priya Singh: If you configure S3 export into your account, you control lifecycle and object policies. Redwood will not keep a secondary copy beyond the configured retention, and we can include contractual language that we won't persist a copy. We'll provide a recommended export pipeline in the docs.

[03:56] Ethan Park: Regarding "no-train" — can we get a signed letter or a clause in the DPA that explicitly states "no training on customer prompts or outputs" and an explanation of what counts as "training"? We've seen vague wording elsewhere.

[04:10] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We can include explicit language: "Redwood will not use customer-supplied prompts, files, or generated outputs as training data for any of Redwood's models or model training pipelines." We'll include the exceptions around anonymized telemetry for platform health and will enumerate those. Leah, will that be sufficient for legal?

[04:26] Leah Brooks: That's a good start. We'll want definitions, and an audit right to validate adherence. Would Redwood allow an independent third-party attestation?

[04:34] Marcus Hale: We're open to a periodic attestation. For Dedicated/Private customers we can run joint audits, and we also have SOC 2 Type II reports for hosted that cover controls around data handling. We can entertain a bespoke attestation for customers with strict needs — we'd scope that separately.

[04:50] Dr. Maya Cortez: Speaking of SOC 2, can you confirm scope — does it include the control environment for encryption key management and change control?

[04:59] Jordan Lee: The SOC 2 covers the control environment for our platform services; key management controls for customer-managed keys are documented in the supplement — though for BYOK the customer KMS is in-scope for the customer. We'll send the SOC 2 Type II and an encryption practice note.

[05:14] Samir Gupta: We operate in the EU; any residency constraints? We need data not to leave EU jurisdiction for certain workloads.

[05:21] Priya Singh: We support region pinning. Hosted can be restricted to EU-only regions, and Private deployment obviously stays on-prem. For Dedicated we can provision capacity in AWS eu-west-1 or GCP europe-west. We'll include a region-by-region data flow diagram.

[05:36] Ethan Park: What about SSO and RBAC? We want least-privilege admin roles and audit logs for admin activity.

[05:43] Marcus Hale: We support SAML 2.0 single sign-on, SCIM provisioning, and role-based controls. There are predefined roles (viewer, developer, admin) and you can create custom roles. All admin actions are logged and we can forward admin audit logs to your SIEM as well.

[05:59] Dr. Maya Cortez: Can you show an example of the audit event for a generation request and an admin role change? We need schema to ingest into our GRC tooling.

[06:09] Priya Singh: Yes — we'll attach sample JSON events. For a generation request we include timestamp, request_id, tenant_id, model_version, token_count, latency_ms, client_ip (anonymized on request), and routing decisions. We do not include prompt text in audit events unless you opt-in to store full-text request logs — which again you control.

[06:28] Leah Brooks: On storing full-text — can we store it in our own S3 and set lifecycle to 30 days? We'll need it for debugging but want short retention.

[06:36] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's a common pattern. We can stream request/response bodies to your S3 bucket; you control lifecycle and access. Redwood will not keep a separate full-text copy beyond any configured short-term retention for live debugging if you choose to enable that.

[06:49] Ethan Park: For the on-prem pilot, what telemetry will you collect? We want to minimize anything leaving our network during the pilot.

[06:57] Marcus Hale: For on-prem pilot we can run in air-gapped or VPC-isolated mode. Telemetry can be completely disabled or limited to local logs that you host. If you want to run remote support, we can do an opt-in debug channel with explicit consent per session.

[07:13] Dr. Maya Cortez: About PHI — our workloads will include lab results. Are there any special controls needed to be HIPAA-compliant? Redwood's product isn't a covered entity, but our use requires BAA-like protections.

[07:24] Priya Singh: We can sign BAA-equivalent terms and configure the platform for PHI — ensure encryption at rest with customer keys, strict RBAC, no-text-retention unless you request it, and audit trail retention. We'll pass along our HIPAA compliance note.

[07:35] Leah Brooks: We'll expect indemnities and breach-notification timing in the agreement.

[07:40] Jordan Lee: Understood, we'll include breach-notice SLAs in the DPA appendix.

[07:44] [00:08 clip — 00:18 speaker overlap — "yeah that's fine" / "sorry go ahead"]

[07:52] Ethan Park: One technical nit — you mentioned the runtime decrypts the data key on the GPU host. Do you support SGX enclaves or a similar isolated execution environment to reduce trust surface?

[08:03] Marcus Hale: We don't currently use SGX for model execution—mostly because of performance tradeoffs and GPU compatibility. Instead we minimize the plaintext window, use strict host hardening, ephemeral instances, and kernel-level protections. For customers that insist on stronger isolation, Private deployments can be configured to run in FIPS/HSM environments with additional attestations.

[08:23] Dr. Maya Cortez: Would Redwood allow a small scope audit for the pilot to confirm keys are not exfiltrated? Preferably an external third-party with limited scope.

[08:33] Jordan Lee: We can scope a limited audit for Dedicated/Private customers. For Hosted customers it's more controlled—SOC2 plus attestations. We'll take a note to scope an audit with you; that'll likely be an additional SOW.

[08:45] Leah Brooks: On the contractual "no-training" clause — will you also include language forbidding downstream model sharing of derived artifacts that include customer data? Like embeddings or fine-tune checkpoints?

[08:58] Priya Singh: Yes — the clause can explicitly forbid use of customer-provided data to create derivative models, embeddings that are shared externally, or fine-tunes that include customer material. For embeddings we treat them as customer data and by default do not share them across tenants.

[09:12] Ethan Park: Are there rate-limits or throttles that could leak usage patterns? We need to prevent timing channels that could reveal PHI or traffic spikes tied to certain clinics.

[09:23] Marcus Hale: Mitigation is possible—request noise, batching, and consistent-latency modes. We can discuss a dedicated capacity profile with smoothing to reduce distinguishability.

[09:33] Dr. Maya Cortez: What about deletion guarantees — if we delete prompts or models, how quickly are they removed from caches and backups?

[09:41] Priya Singh: Deletion follows a pipeline: caches cleared immediately, active replicas dropped, and then background jobs scrub short-term backups within a 24-72 hour window by default; longer retention backups depend on your configured retention. For strict no-residual data needs we can accelerate the scrub and provide attestation.

[09:59] [crosstalk slightly] Jordan Lee: Quick pause — we have a few links I'll share: SOC2 report (link), security-datasheet.pdf (link), KMS architecture diagram (link), sample audit events (link).

[10:12] Priya Singh: I'll also include a short playbook for the pilot — steps for network setup, KMS wiring, and how to capture logs in your SIEM.

[10:20] Dr. Maya Cortez: Sounds good. A few more clarifying Qs — do you retain model snapshots? If we lock to a model version, can Redwood upgrade it without our permission?

[10:31] Marcus Hale: Customers can pin model versions; Redwood will not force upgrades without a defined rollout plan. For Hosted we recommend managed updates but you can request pinned versions for certain tenants. Any upgrade that could affect outputs would go through a canary and you'd be informed.

[10:45] Ethan Park: Regarding exportability — if we decide to leave Redwood, can we export logs, embeddings, and a copy of model prompts? How long will you hold data for the export window?

[10:56] Jordan Lee: Upon contract termination we provide a 30-day export window by default; that can be extended. We'll produce exported artifacts in a structured format and then purge tenant data per the DPA.

[11:07] Leah Brooks: Do you support data residency in a specific EU country? Our legal prefers data to remain in Germany.

[11:14] Priya Singh: Region pinning to Germany (eu-central-1) is supported on Dedicated or Private. Hosted in the EU we can prefer eu-central-1 but would check availability and capacity. We'll include a region-availability matrix.

[11:27] Samir Gupta: Are PII detection/redaction hooks available inline? We might want an optional preprocessor that scrubs or tokenizes PHI before it reaches the model.

[11:36] Marcus Hale: We have an optional pre-processing plugin that can mask or hash identifiable fields. For Private deployments you can supply your own scrubbing pipeline that runs before inference. For Hosted we offer configurable redaction templates and a compliance pipeline.
trailer: [46:30] Recap & next steps: Jordan will send SOC2 and security docs; Priya will deliver KMS POC notes and sample audit events; schedule pilot week of 2026-05-25; Vespertine legal to send DPA redlines. Meeting closed at ~15:48 UTC.
